name: Herbicide injury — clomazone-type bleaching
summary: A documented hemp chemical-injury differential in which soil-residual clomazone caused severe bleaching of newly formed tissue. The image pattern is not enough to identify the active ingredient; exposure history is essential.
indicators: Newly formed tissue becomes markedly bleached after a plausible herbicide carryover or drift event
Multiple plants share an exposure-pattern distribution in the field or production area
Symptoms begin after a documented chemical application, carryover, contaminated medium, or drift event
exclusions: Iron or sulfur deficiency is analytically supported and follows a root-zone pattern
Mites or systemic pathogens explain deformation and discoloration better
Bleaching maps tightly to high-light exposure rather than chemical distribution

progression.description: Plants encounter residual or drifted herbicide.
New tissue loses normal pigmentation and becomes bleached.
Growth can remain strongly impaired; the documented clomazone field case did not recover.

confirmation: Reconstruct spray, carryover, neighboring-field, substrate, and water-treatment history.
Use field pattern, timing, and where available laboratory residue analysis; do not identify clomazone from color alone.
immediateActions: Stop further suspected exposure and preserve records of all recent chemical applications.
Separate exposure investigation from nutrient correction so evidence is not erased.
correctivePlan: Address the confirmed exposure source and follow crop-specific professional guidance for affected plants and contaminated media/soil.
prevention: Maintain chemical-use records and review previous-crop residual restrictions before planting hemp.
Protect production areas from drift and contaminated equipment.
warnings: Bleached new growth is not clomazone-specific.
This profile does not recommend herbicide use; it is an injury-identification differential.

sources.title: Surveying for Potential Diseases and Abiotic Disorders of Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Production
supportedClaims: North Carolina hemp diagnostic submissions included root binding, excess water, nutrient disorders, and herbicide injury as important abiotic differentials.

Root-bound transplants were commonly reported and affected plants did not reliably overcome the bound root system after field transplanting; secondary Fusarium and Pythium infections were also observed.
Clomazone carryover caused bleaching of newly formed hemp tissue in a documented commercial field case and the plants did not recover.

Field and diagnostic observations also documented manganese toxicity as interveinal yellowing followed by interveinal necrosis, supporting it as a real hemp differential but not a camera-only diagnosis.
